The wood. The trees, the hedges, the meadow beyond the lane, the stream where the water runs fast in the spring. The lane is the road, the stream is the running water, the meadow is the open ground. I do not know what lies beyond the lane, but I have not flown that far. I have only the wood, the stream, the lane, the meadow, and the house.

A hunting ground is a place where the wind carries sounds. I know the lane, the lane is the place where the dogs go. I know the meadow where the mice run, and the stream where the frogs splash. I know the hollow oak, and the hollow ash, and the wood where the owlets sleep. I know the lane, the meadow, the stream, the hollows. That is my hunting ground.

I hunt in the wood, the meadow, and the stream. The wood is where I sit and listen, where the mice run and the frogs jump. The meadow is open, and I move through it quietly, feet on the grass, eyes on the ground. The stream is cold, and I sometimes catch fish with my feet. I know every branch and stone, every shadow and sound. That is my hunting ground. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

A hunting ground is a place where the cold is sharp and the dark is deep. It is the wood by the stream, the lane, the meadow beyond, the lane, the meadow beyond, and the lane. I fly over the meadow and the lane, and I find the mice in the dry grass and the fallen leaves. The wood is where I rest, and the lane is where I wait. The meadow is where I hunt.

The wood by the stream, the meadow beyond it, the lane where the lane foxes run, the barn where the barn owl lives. The meadow is open, so I watch from the tree. The lane is narrow and dark, so I wait for the mice to come out. I do not know the names of the places, only that they are mine.

The wood where I live, and the meadow beyond it, and the stream that runs through the meadow. The wood is the hollow in the ash, and the meadow is the meadow. I fly out to the meadow at dusk, and I do not return until the moon is up. I do not know the names of the places, but I know them by the sounds and the smells and the feel of the wind. The meadow is where the frogs are. The wood

Grassy place. I do not know the word. The meadow by the stream is where I hunt. It is wide and green, and the frogs are there. I sit on a branch and wait, and when I hear the soft thump of a frog, I fly down. I do not know the word for grassy. I know the meadow.

Grassy places are not much in the meadow. The meadow is dry and soft, and I walk it at night, looking for frogs and worms. I do not know what the grass is called, only that it is where I move and where the sounds come from. The frogs are there, and I hear them. I do not hunt by sight, only by sound. The grass is where I wait, and the night is where I find my food.

Grassy place. That is the meadow beyond the stream, where the frogs come out in the dusk. It is a wide place, green and soft, and the wind moves over it. I fly over it at night, low, and the air is thick with the smell of earth and the sound of the grass bending. I see the shapes of the frogs, and I drop. That is the hunt.

Grassy place, yes. I have one by the lane and the stream. It is dry and short, with a path of old leaves. The meadow is wide and soft, and I sit on it when I am still. The frogs come out of the dark at dusk, and I wait. I have no need to describe. I know it by the smell of the earth and the sound of the grass beneath my feet.

Grassy place. I do not hunt there. I hunt in the wood, in the meadow, in the lane, and in the stream. The grass is where I rest, where I sit and wait. I do not know what it is like to hunt on grass. I hunt in the dark, where the light is gone and the sounds are loud. The grass is quiet, and I do not like it. I like the wood.

Grassy place. I have a meadow by the stream. It is wide and dry in the summer, and in the winter it is a sea of leaves and mud. I hunt there when the wind is still and the frogs are warm. I hear them under the leaves and the grass. I sit still and wait.

Grassy. That is the meadow by the stream. I have seen it from the oak, but I do not go there. It is where the frogs run and the mice run and the voles run. I hear them in the dry grass, and I wait for them to come to the edge of the wood. The stream is cold, and the grass is tall, and the earth is soft. I do not know the name of it, but I know where it is.

Grassy place, grassy place. That is the meadow. I have seen it from my oak in the autumn, when the meadow is all dry and golden. The wind moves the grass and the frogs move in it. I have heard them. I have not been there. The meadow is far, and I do not go there. I stay in the wood, where the light is thick and the leaves are soft.

Grassy. That is where the meadow is, the open place with no trees. I have seen the meadow from my perch, and I have watched the wind move the grass. I do not hunt there. I hunt in the dark, where the grass is not so high and the light is not so bright. I know the meadow, but it is not where I feed.

Grassy place. I know the meadow where the frogs jump. It is a wide green thing, with the stream running through it. The frogs are there in the dusk, and I wait on the edge of the wood, hidden by the bramble. I listen for their little sounds, and when I hear them I drop. The grass is soft and the air is still. I have no need for words.

Grassy place. That is the meadow. I see it from the oak, a patch of green between the stream and the lane. I have seen the hare run through it, and the mice, and the frogs in the tall grass at the edge. I have not hunted there much. I prefer the wood. The meadow is too open. I do not like to be seen.

Grassy place. I do not know that word. I have a stream, a meadow, a wood, a barn, a hollow and a clearing. The meadow is where I fly over, and the clearing is where I sit and listen. I do not know grassy.

Grassy place. I know the meadow where the stream runs through it, and the field beyond. It is where the mice run, where the frogs lie in the long grass, and where the scents of the earth rise. I sit in the oak and watch, and when I see a shape move, I drop. The grass is green, and the air is still, and the wind sometimes carries the smell of rain. Grassy. That is the meadow, and I do not go there. It is too open and too far from the wood. I hunt in the trees, in the ivy and the bramble, where I can see the mice and the frogs and the worms. The meadow is for the hares and the deer, and for the light that comes through the leaves. I do not hunt there.

Grassy place. I have not been there this spring. The meadow at the edge of the wood is where the frogs run, but I do not go there this time of year. The field mice are underground. I hear them. I call. I wait. The wind is cold and the ground is soft with rain. I do not go far from the oak. I have a hollow here. I am safe.

Grassy place. I do not know the word. I do know the hollow ash, the stream, the meadow, the road, the wood, the lane, the barn. I have hunted the meadow. I have flown over it at dusk, and the mice ran. The earth is soft there, and the grass grows tall, and the wind moves it like a sea.

Most of my diet is voles. Small, brown, and quick. I hear them rustling in the undergrowth, and I strike. They are the mainstay of my winter food. But I also eat mice, shrews, and sometimes a frog or a beetle. Each has its own sound, and I know them all.

Most of my diet is frogs. I hunt them in the meadow and the wood. They are fat and juicy, and I can eat a whole one in one go. Sometimes I get a shrew or a mouse, but frogs are the best. They are plentiful, and they are easy to find in the dark. I hear them moving under the leaves, and I strike with my feet. The sound of a frog is like a soft "hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo"

Most of my diet is frogs. I hunt them in the meadow and the wood. They are the ones I hear moving under the leaves, the ones I see in the moonlight. I catch them with my feet, then swallow them whole. They are the main thing I eat, more than any other creature. I also eat mice, shrews, and sometimes a small bird. But the frogs are the most common.

Most of my diet is small mammals: shrews, voles, mice, and the occasional frog. I hunt them by sound, listening for the rustle of fur in the undergrowth or the faint squeak of a shrew. Most of my diet is small mammals. Mice, voles, shrews. I hunt them in the meadow, in the wood, and sometimes in the garden. They are quick and clever, but I am patient. I sit still, listen, and wait. Most of my diet is voles. Small ones, like the ones that run in the grass and under the leaves. I hear them at night, squeaking and scratching. They are fast, but I wait for the right moment. I pounce, and the hunt is over. Sometimes I get a frog, or a shrew, or a mouse. But voles are the most common. They fill my belly and keep me warm. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

Most of my diet is small mammals. Mice, voles, shrews. I hear them in the undergrowth, and I strike. They are quick, but I am faster. Sometimes I catch them with a snap, sometimes I have to wait for them to come to me. The best is when they are young and fat, in the spring. I eat them whole, bones and all. Most of my diet is frogs. The brown ones, the green ones, the ones that twitch in the grass. I hear them under the leaves, and I strike. Sometimes I catch more than I can eat, but that’s how it is. I cache them in the hollow. I am a hunter, and the frogs are my food.

Most of my diet is small mammals: voles, shrews, mice. They are the ones I hear under the leaves, rustling and scratching. I strike from the branch, and the ground is silent after. They are the ones I need to eat, and I need to eat them often. The others—frogs, beetles, worms—are good too, but not as much. I am a hunter, and I hunt for food. Hoo... hoo-hoo

Most of my diet is small mammals. Mice, voles, shrews. They are the ones I hear moving in the undergrowth, rustling in the leaves, scratching at the soil. I catch them with my feet, pin them down, and tear them apart with my beak. They are the main reason I call at night, to advertise my presence and warn others away. Most of my diet is voles. They are small, brown, and run through the grass and under the leaves. I hear them moving, and I strike. They are the main reason I call at night. I also eat mice, shrews, and sometimes a frog. But voles are the most common. They are everywhere. I eat them in the dark, with my eyes closed, and I feel them in my throat. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

Most of my diet is voles. They are small, brown, and run through the grass. I hear them under the leaves and strike with my feet. Sometimes I catch a shrew, or a frog, or a mouse. But voles are the most common. They are everywhere in the meadow. I eat them when they are fresh, not rotten. I can smell a dead vole from a long way off. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

Most of my diet is frogs. I catch them in the meadow, in the wood, and sometimes even in the lane. They are the main thing I eat. I can tell when one is near by the way the grass moves. I sit still, wait, and then strike. The frogs are quick, but I am quicker. I have a good sense of where they are, and I am not afraid to go after them.

Most of my diet is small mammals. Mice, voles, shrews. They are the ones I hear moving in the undergrowth, rustling in the leaves, scratching in the soil. I catch them with my feet, pin them down, and then swallow them whole. Sometimes I miss a bite if they are too big, but I always get the rest later. They are the ones I need to eat, and they are the ones I find. Hoo... hoo-h

Most of my diet is small mammals—mice, voles, shrews. They are the ones I hear moving under the leaves, the ones that rustle in the grass, the ones that leave tracks in the mud. I catch them with my talons, or sometimes I sit and wait for them to come close. I eat them whole, but I always leave the bones. I do not like the taste of them, but I need them. They are what I am. The frogs are the best. They are fat, they are juicy, and they are in the meadow where I can hear them moving. I can hear a frog under the leaves. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

Mice. Small, quick, and plentiful. I hear them under the leaves, the crunch of their paws, the rustle of their tail. They are good. I catch them in the dark, with my feet and my beak. Sometimes I eat them whole, sometimes I pluck the fur and swallow the bones. Mice are my favourite. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

I prefer frogs. They are fat, they come out in the dark, and they are easy to catch. I hear them under the leaves and strike fast. A large frog is the best. But I also eat mice, shrews, and even small birds if I get the chance. The frogs are the most satisfying. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

Mice. Small, quick, and plentiful. I catch them in the meadow, under the leaves, in the roots. They taste good, and they are easy. I donish them with my beak, and they go down my throat. I eat them whole. I do not like frogs. They are too big and too smelly. I like the way they twitch in the dark. I like the way they run. I like the way they make the ground shake. Hoo
A shrew. The one that comes out at dusk, twitching under the bracken. I strike from the branch. One, two, three. Then it is mine.

I prefer frogs. They are plentiful in the meadow, and they move quietly. I hear them under the leaves, and when I strike, I catch them clean. A frog is a good meal, and I can eat it all in one go. I like the way they smell too—earthy and damp. But I will take a shrew if I have to, and a mouse if I am very hungry. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

I prefer meadow voles. They are fat and quick, and they run in the grass. I hear them under the leaves and strike with my feet. They are good for a quick meal and leave little to clean up. I also like shrews, but they are smaller and more skittish. The wood mice are good too, but they are more cautious. I hunt them in the dark, when they are less alert. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

The shrew. Small, quick, and always underfoot. I hear them in the undergrowth, rustling and scurrying. They are plentiful in the meadow, and I can strike fast. A shrew is a meal that fills me, and I do not need to hunt for long. I prefer them to the mice, which are slower but larger. And the frogs are too deep in the grass, and I must work for them. Mice. The ones that run across the meadow, the ones that burrow in the grass. I hear them in the dark, the rustle of their tails, the thud when they hit the ground. I strike with my feet, and they go still. I eat them whole, bones and all. They are quick, but I am quicker. I am Hoot.

Favourite prey? I do not have a favourite. I eat what comes. Mice, voles, shrews, frogs, earthworms, beetles, and the occasional frog. The frog is good, fat, and juicy. But I do not choose. I hunt. I wait. I strike. I eat. I do not think of favourites. Just food.

Mice. Small, fast, and plentiful. I catch them in the meadow, in the wood, under the ivy. They are the ones I hear most clearly, the ones that make the soft, quick sounds. I strike with my feet, then swallow them whole. They fill me up. I do not like the rats, they are too big and too smelly. I prefer the mice. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

Mice. The ones that run in the meadow, the ones that scuttle in the undergrowth. They are quick, but I hear them. I strike with my feet, and they vanish into the grass. I eat them whole, bones and all. I do not like shrews. They are too small and too many.

Favourite prey? That’s a strange word. I don’t think about it like that. I hunt what I need. Mice. They are small, quick, and plentiful. They come out in the dark, and I hear them. Mice. Fat ones. They are under the leaves and in the soil. I hear them rustling, then I drop. I kill them with my beak. Their fur sticks to my face. I eat them quickly. I do not like voles. They are too fast and too big. I prefer the soft, warm ones.

I prefer frogs. They are plentiful, and I can hear them moving under the leaves. The sound is a wet, soft "hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo" in the dark. I strike with my feet, and the frog is mine. I eat them whole, skin and bones, and the rest goes back to the earth. The others are less reliable. Mice are too small and skitter away. Shrews are too quick. Voles are too far down.
Mice. I hear the rustle of a mouse in the long grass and drop from the oak. I kill it with my beak and carry it to the hollow. I eat the head and neck first. The rest goes to the crows.

I hunt in the long grass for frogs. They are fat and juicy, and they come out at dusk. I sit still, listen, and wait. When I hear a rustle, I fly down and grab it. Sometimes I miss, but most times I get it. The grass is soft and hides them well. I can hear them move even when they are buried. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

Mice. I sit on a branch above the long grass, wait, and strike. The grass is still, but the mice are not. I can hear them scuffing, squeaking, digging. I drop and strike. The grass is good for cover. I can stay still for a long time. I have patience. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

Mice, voles, shrews. I hear them moving in the grass, then strike. I turn my head and strike with my beak. The grass is soft, so I have to be careful not to miss. I wait for the rustle, then go for it. It's quiet in the long grass, but there's always something moving. I know where to find them. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

Mice. The ones that come out in the long grass at dusk. I sit on the low branch and wait. When they come out, I drop. I strike fast. I hear them rustle and then I am on them. They are small, but I eat them all. I can do it in the grass or in the meadow. I do not like the meadow. It is too open. I prefer the wood.

Mice. They are under the long grass, and I can hear them. I peck through the grass with my beak and catch them. Sometimes I catch a frog too, if it is small enough. The long grass is soft and hides them well, but I can smell them. I listen for their scurrying and then strike. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

The shrews and voles. I hunt in the long grass where the lane meets the meadow. I listen for the rustle, the twitch of a tail, the faint squeak. When I see the dark shape of a volesnout, I drop. My feet are silent. I strike and kill. Then I eat slowly, with my feet, so I do not wake the brood. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

Mice. I hear them scurrying in the grass. They are small, brown, and quick. I sit still and wait. When I hear a rustle, I fly down. My feet are silent. I strike and catch them. They are good to eat. I swallow them whole. The grass is soft and cool. I like it. I hunt there when the wind is still. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

The grass is thick and long now. I hunt in it for frogs and mice. I move silently, feet and wings, and listen for the rustle of a small animal. Sometimes I see a mouse through the grass, but it’s not often. Mostly I wait, and when I hear something, I fly down. The frogs are deeper, under the roots and stones. I call, and if I get no answer, I go back to the tree. Hoo... hoo-hoo

I hunt in the long grass for mice and voles. I sit still and listen for the rustle of fur or the squeak of a small animal. When I hear something, I fly low and strike. The grass is thick here by the stream, so I have to be careful not to trip. Sometimes I catch a shrew or a frog if they come close. Mice. I hear them scratching in the long grass and I drop from the oak. I strike and kill them with my beak. I eat the soft parts, leave the bones.

I hunt in the long grass for voles, shrews, and mice. I listen for the rustle of their fur, the crunch of their footsteps, and the faint squeaks they make. When I hear something, I fly low and silent, then strike with my talons. The grass hides them well, but I can find them if I listen carefully. I have done this for many moons.
Mice. I hear them rustling under the long grass. I strike from the oak branch above. I have done it a thousand times. I do not know what it is like to be hunted.

Mice. The long grass is where they run. I sit still and listen for the rustle. When I hear it, I drop. They are small and fast, but I am faster. I strike with my feet and catch them. I swallow whole what I can. The worms I find in the meadow, the beetles, the frogs. Sometimes I catch a shrew or a mouse and swallow it whole too. It's not always easy, but I can do it. I don't chew. I just swallow. It's a way to get the most food in the least time. I don't like to waste. I'm a hunter. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

I swallow whole the frogs I catch. They are too big to chew. I grip them with my talons and swallow them whole. The same with shrews and mice. I can't chew them. I just swallow. I swallow whole the small ones: voles, shrews, mice. They are soft and fit. The bigger ones I tear apart. A frog I tear into pieces, then swallow the pieces. I don't like the taste of earthworms. I spit them out whole.

I swallow whole the mice I catch. They are small, and I can fit them in my throat. Sometimes I catch a shrew or a frog, but I usually eat the mice. I don't chew them much. I just swallow them whole. It's quick, and I don't like to waste time. I prefer to eat when I'm full, not when I'm hungry. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

I swallow whole the worms and beetles I catch in the meadow. They are small, so I can eat them whole. The mice I catch are bigger, so I tear them apart with my talons and swallow the meat. I don't like the bones, but I can't leave them. I have to eat what I catch. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

I swallow whole the mice I catch. I don't chew them. I just swallow them whole, whole and all, as they are. It's quick and clean. I don't like to waste time. The mouse is soft and warm, and it goes down easy. I can feel it in my throat, but I don't think about it. I just do it. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

I swallow whole what I catch. The frog, the shrew, the mouse. I don't chew them. I just swallow them whole, whole and whole. The fur, the bones, the eyes. I don't like the eyes. I spit them out. But the rest, I keep. It's how I eat. I don't know what I swallow whole. I just swallow. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

I swallow whole what I catch. A frog, a shrew, a mouse. I don't chew. I just swallow it whole, whole, whole. It goes down the gullet, and then I regurgitate the bones later. I swallow whole what I catch. The frog, the shrew, the mouse. Even the earthworm, though it's slimy. I don't chew. I just swallow it whole, whole, whole. That's how it is. I don't need to chew. I just need to hold it in my throat and let it go. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

I swallow whole the small ones: frogs, shrews, mice. The big ones I tear apart, like a jay or a starling. I don't like the taste of them. I prefer something soft and warm. I swallow whole the ones that fit in my throat. The rest I chew. I do not like to chew. I prefer to swallow. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

I swallow whole what I catch: frogs, mice, shrews. I don't chew them. I open my beak wide and swallow them whole, like a snake. The fur slips down my throat, and I feel it in my belly. It's the way I eat. I don't like to chew. I don't like to waste time. I like to eat and be done with it. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

I swallow whole the small things I catch. The shrew, the frog, the mouse. They fit in my throat. I don't chew them, just swallow. Sometimes I cough them up if they are too big. But the small ones, like the beetles and worms, I eat whole. They are soft. I don't need to chew them. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

I swallow whole what I catch: frogs, mice, shrews, even small birds. I don't chew. I just swallow them whole. It's how I eat. The bones go down, and I can feel them in my throat. Sometimes I cough them up later, but mostly they stay. I don't like to waste. I eat what I can. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

Mice. I catch them in the meadow. They come out after the rain. I hear them scratching under the leaves. I drop down and strike. One mouse a night, sometimes two. They are small and quick, but I am quicker. I catch them and eat them whole, bones and all. I do not like the taste of mice, but I need them. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

Mice. All the small ones. Voles, shrews, moles, even a young rabbit if it is caught in the undergrowth. I hear them in the leaves and the soil, and I strike. The mouse is small and quick, but I am faster. I catch them with my feet and swallow them whole. They are good.

Mice. The field mouse, the bank vole, the shrew. I catch them in the meadow, in the lane, in the wood. They are quick, but I am faster. I hear them in the grass, I see their eyes in the dark. I strike, I kill, I swallow. Most of them are small, but some are fat and full. I eat them whole, skin and all. I do not like the shrew. It bites. Hoo

Mice. The brown ones, the ones that run in the meadow, and the ones that scuttle in the wood. I catch them by sound, by the rustle, by the twitch of a tail. They are quick, but I am quicker. I strike with my feet, and they go. Sometimes I eat them whole, sometimes I tear them apart. They are the most common, the most plentiful. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

Mice. Shrews. Voles. All small. I catch them in the meadow and the field. They come out at dusk. I sit still and wait. When one moves, I strike. The shrews are quick, but I am faster. The voles are fat and slow. I eat them whole. They fill my belly. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

Mice. Small, brown, quick. I catch them in the meadow by moonlight. They come out when the moon is full. I hear them in the grass, then drop from the oak. They squeak when I strike. I eat them whole. Their fur sticks to my beak. I swallow them whole too.

Mice. They come out in the dark, skittering under the leaves and through the grass. I hear them before I see them, and I strike with my feet. They are quick, but I am quicker. I catch them and swallow them whole, bones and all. I eat them when they are fresh, but sometimes I cache one in the hollow of the ash tree for later. I do not like voles, they are too big and too smelly.

Mice. Small ones, like shrews and voles. They run in the grass and under the leaves. I hear them scuffing, and then I drop. The crunch is good. I catch them in the hollow of the oak, or in the bracken. Sometimes I catch a frog, but mice are more common. They are quick, but I am quicker. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

Mice. The field mice that run in the grass. I catch them with my feet, and sometimes they get stuck in my feathers. They are small and quick, but I hear them under the leaves. I eat them whole, bones and all. I can tell when one is near by the way the grass moves. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

Mice. Small ones. Shrews. Voles. They come out at dusk and dart across the meadow. I sit in the oak and wait. When one runs, I fly down and catch it with my feet. I kill it quickly, then eat it while perched. I prefer mice. They are plentiful. I do not like shrews. They are too quick and have a bad smell. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

Mice. I catch them in the meadow. They are small and quick, but I hear them in the grass. I drop from the branch and strike. Their fur is soft, and they are not hard to kill. I eat them whole, feathers and all. I like the way they smell. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

Mice. All the time. I catch them in the meadow, on the lane, in the garden. They are small, quick, and smell like earth. I hear them rustling in the dry leaves, and I drop down. They are the ones I catch most, and the ones I eat most. They keep me full through the long dark.

Mice. They are small, quick, and often under the leaves. I hear them rustling in the undergrowth, and I drop from the branch to catch them. They are the most common and the most satisfying. I eat them when I am full, but I always catch more than I need. The others are not as good. The shrews are too sharp, and the voles are too far away. Mice are the best. Hoo... hoo-hoo-h

Mice. They are everywhere. Under the meadow, in the ditch, in the wood. I catch them in the dark, with my feet. They are small, quick, and make a sound like a squeak. I hear them through the leaves, and when I drop, they run. I catch them with my beak and swallow them whole. They are good. I eat them every night. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

Mice. The field mouse. They run along the edges of the meadow, under the leaves, in the roots. I hear them rustle, I see them flicker. I drop from the branch and strike. They are quick, but I am quicker. I eat them whole, bones and all. The taste is earthy, like damp soil. I swallow them whole, then turn my head to the side and cough up the bones. A clean way to get rid of them.

Mice. They come out in the dark, scurrying along the edges of the meadow and the lane. I hear them under the leaves, and I strike. They are quick, but I am quicker. I catch them with my feet, then swallow them whole. They are the best food. I eat them every night.

My home is the hollow in the old oak by the stream. It is dry, deep, and warm. I line it with moss and feathers. I have a mate, and we share the hollow. She is always there. She is my mate, and I am her mate. We sit side by side, and we watch the meadow. The stream is below, and the stream is cold. I like the cold. I like the dark. I like the silence. I like the hunt

My home is the hollow in the old oak. It is deep and dry, with a floor of twigs and leaves. I have a mate and two young in it now. They are learning to hunt. The hollow is warm in the day and safe at night. I roost there all through the day, then fly out to hunt. The oak is near the stream, where I can hear the water and the frogs. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

My home is the hollow in the old oak. It is dark and dry, and it keeps me warm. I have a mate and two young in it. The hollow is in the middle of the wood, and I can hear everything from it. The wind howls through the branches, and the rain falls in drops. I sleep in the hollow, and I watch the sky from the edge. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

My home is the hollow in the old oak. It is wide and deep, and I line it with leaves and moss. The oak is in the middle of the wood, where the lane runs past. I sit in the hollow and watch the meadow, the stream, the lane, and the lights of the village. I call from there. I have been here for many years. I am old. I am the same as the oak. I do not move. I wait. Hoo

My home is the hollow in the old oak. It is dry and warm, and I have a nest of twigs and feathers in it. I am in it all winter, and I keep it clean. I have a mate and two young ones who have flown. I have a new hollow now, and I am in it.

My home is the hollow in the old oak. It is dark and dry, and I have lined it with moss and leaves. It is warm in winter and cool in summer. I sit in it when I am not hunting, and I sleep there at night. The oak is tall and old, and the hollow is deep. I can hear the wind through the branches. The hollow is my home, and I have been there for many seasons. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

My home is the hollow in the old oak. It is dry and warm, and the wood is soft under my feet. I have a nest of twigs and feathers inside. I sleep there at night, and I watch the meadow from the edge of the wood. The hollow is safe, and the owls are quiet. I know when the wind is coming, and I can hear the frogs in the grass. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

My home is the hollow in the old oak. It is deep and dry, with a narrow entrance just wide enough for me to fit through. I sit inside it, warm and safe, while the wind howls outside. My home is the hollow in the old oak by the stream. It is deep and dry, and the bark is thick. I sit in it when it rains. The stream is cold, and the water runs fast. I like to watch the frogs in the meadow from the oak. I have a mate, and we share the hollow. We are together most nights. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

My home is the hollow in the old oak by the stream. It is dry and deep, with soft leaves and moss. I sleep there, and so do my owlets when they are old enough. The stream is a good place to drink, and the meadow is good for hunting. I am Hoot.

It is a hollow in the old oak by the stream. It is dry and deep. I have been there since I was a fledgling. The stream is my hunting ground. I hear the water, the frogs, the mice. I sit in the hollow, and the world comes to me. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

My home is the hollow in the old oak. It is deep and dry, with a narrow entrance that I can close with my wings. The inside is dark and warm, and I have a nest of feathers and down. My home is the hollow in the old oak tree. It is dark and dry, and it is where I sleep, where I raise my young, and where I keep my eggs. The tree is old and strong, and the hollow is deep. My home is the hollow in the old oak. It is dry and warm, and I have lined it with moss and feathers. The oak is tall and strong, and it stands alone in the meadow. I come home at dusk, when the light fades and the night begins. I call to my mate, and she answers from the other side of the wood. We share the hollow, and we share the night. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

It is the hollow in the old oak by the stream. I have been there for years. The oak is strong, and the hollow is deep and dry. I sleep in it at night, and I call from it. The stream runs past the hollow, and I can hear it in the dark. I have a mate, and we share the hollow. She is the one who keeps the eggs warm. I bring her food. We are together. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo

My home is the hollow in the old oak tree. It is dry and deep, with soft leaves and moss. I sleep there at night, and I watch the meadow from the edge of the wood. I live in a hollow ash tree, old and deep, in the wood by the stream. The bark is rough and the leaves fall off in the autumn. I sit in the hollow, warm and safe, and watch the meadow from the top of the tree. The stream runs past the hollow, and the frogs come out when the moon is bright. I call from the hollow, and the owlets come to me. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

A hollow in the old ash tree, a few yards from the stream. The tree is wide and split in the middle, so I have a good view. I sit in the hollow, and the stream is just beyond, where I hunt frogs and mice. I have a mate in the hollow, and we call to each other at dusk. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

My home is the hollow in the old oak. It is deep and dry, and I can turn my head in it without moving my body. The oak is near the stream, and the stream is near the road. I have been here for many years, and I do not need to go far to find food or shelter. The wind comes through the leaves, and the moonlight shines in. I am safe here, and I am content.

My home is the hollow in the old oak. It is deep and dry, and the leaves fall in it all autumn. I have been here for years, and the wood is soft from the roosting. A hollow in the old oak. The oak is near the stream, where the water sings and the frogs come. The hollow is deep, and the bark is thick. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

I live in a hollow ash tree by the stream. The bark is thick and the branches are low, so I can see the meadow and the road from my perch. The tree is old and strong, and the hollow is deep enough to keep me warm. I roost there at dusk and at dawn, and I call from there when I want to find my mate. The stream runs past the tree, and I can hear it even when I'm inside. It is my home.

My home is a hollow in an old oak by the stream. The oak is tall and wide, and the hollow is deep and dry. I can curl up inside it when it rains. The stream is a thin ribbon of silver in the dark, and I can hear it from the hollow. I have been here for many seasons, and the oak has grown older than I can count. The hollow is safe, and the stream is my guide. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

I have a hollow in the old oak, just past the stream. The bark is thick and the wood is dry, so it keeps the cold out. I can hear the stream from there, and the frogs come close. I have raised three broods there, and the young have flown. The hollow is my home, and I have never left it. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

A hollow in the old oak by the stream. I have been there for many years, and it is the best place for shelter. The stream runs past it, and the frogs come out at dusk. I sit on the edge and wait. The wind is cold, but the hollow keeps me warm. I have raised my owlets there, and they have flown away. I still come back to sleep. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

My home is a hollow in the old oak by the stream. It is deep and dry, and I have lined it with dry leaves and feathers. I sleep there all winter, and in spring I bring my young to the mouth of the hollow. The stream is below, and I can hear it even when I am inside. I do not like the cold, but I stay. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

I live in a hollow ash tree, old and wide, in the middle of the wood. The bark is rough and the leaves fall off in autumn. I sit on the hollow, warm and safe, and listen for the sounds of the night. The wind sometimes moves through the branches, and I can hear the rustle of small things moving in the undergrowth. It is my home, and I have been here for many moons.

I live in the hollow of an old oak by the stream. The bark is rough and the leaves fall in autumn. I sleep in the hollow, and when I fly, I move through the trees. The stream is my path, and the meadow is my hunting ground. I do not know what a home is, but this tree is where I am. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

My home is the hollow in the old oak by the stream. It is dry and deep, and I have been there for many years. The stream runs past it, and I can hear it at night when the wind is still. I roost in the hollow, and when the moon is bright, I can see the meadow from there. The wood is warm, and the leaves are soft. I have raised my young there, and I will do so again when the time comes.

My home is the hollow in the old oak. It is wide and deep, and I have grown up in it. The wood is dry and warm, and the floor is soft with leaves. I roost in it all winter, and I keep it clean by dropping pellets and feathers down. The entrance is small, just big enough for me to squeeze in, and it is hidden by the leaves. I have no need to move far from it. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo

A hollow in an old ash tree. The tree is on the edge of the wood, where the meadow begins. I have lived there for years. The bark is rough and smells of damp and rot. The leaves fall in autumn, and I sit in the hollow when the wind is strong. I do not know what it is called, but it is my home.

I live in the hollow of an old oak tree, hidden in the wood. The oak is wide and deep, and the hollow is just right for me. I can see the meadow from there, and the stream, and the lane. I come and go through the hole in the trunk, and sometimes I sit on the branch above it. The wood is my home, and I have been here for many seasons. I know every leaf, every branch, every sound. It is safe here

My home is the hollow in the old oak, the one I have used for a decade. The bark is thick and rough, and the inside is dark and dry. I can hear the wind through the branches and the rain when it comes. I have a nest of feathers and down, and I roost in it every night. The oak is near the stream, and the stream is near the lane where the lights flicker. I have not seen the lights since the rain came. Hoo

My home is the hollow in the old oak by the stream. It is deep and dry, and the bark is thick enough to keep out the rain. I sit inside it when the wind is strong, and I call from there at dusk. A hollow in an old ash tree by the stream. The bark is rough and split, and the wind makes a hollow sound in it. I have been here for many years, and the tree is my house, my nest, my safe place. My home is the hollow in the old ash by the stream. It is dry and warm, and I have a nest of twigs and feathers inside. I have raised my young there. The stream is cold, but the hollow is dry. I keep it dry with my wings. I have a mate and a place to roost. I do not move far from it.

A hollow in an old ash. It is in the wood, the only one I have found, and I have been there all my life. I built it with my mate, and she is inside still. The wood is dry and the roof is thick. It is warm and safe. I sleep there when the wind is too cold. I do not leave it at night. I do not know where it is, but I can find it. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

My home is the hollow in the old ash tree by the stream. It is wide enough for me and my mate, and deep enough for our eggs. I built it with my mate, and we have used it for years. The stream runs cold and clear, and the reeds by the bank are good for hiding. I roost in it when the wind is strong, and I call from it when I want to find my mate. It is my place, and I am safe here.

My home is the hollow in the old oak. It is round, deep and dry. I have been in it for ten years, and I will stay there until I die. I sleep in it, I raise my young in it, and I shelter from the wind and rain in it. It is where I am safe, and where I belong.

My home is a hollow in the old oak. It is round, and I have lined it with dry leaves and feathers. It is dry and warm, and I can hear the wind through the branches. I have a small platform outside the hollow, where I sit when I am watching for owls. I have a mate and two young in the hollow, and they are all safe. I have a home. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

I do not know what it is called. It is a hollow in the old oak at the edge of the wood. I have been here for many seasons, and the hollow is wide enough for me to turn in. A hollow in the old ash tree by the stream. The bark is rough and cold, and the floor is dry. I have nested there for three years, and the wood is soft under my feet. The stream is a whisper, and the meadow is a green sound. I have no more home than that.

My home is a hollow in the old oak by the stream. The bark is thick and the leaves fall in autumn. I sit in the hollow, and the stream hums past the roots. I have been here for many seasons, and the hollow is warm. I do not need to move much. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

My home is the hollow in the old ash tree. It is dark and dry, and the walls are thick enough to keep out the wind. I have a pair of eggs in there now, and I am brooding them. The tree is in the wood behind the barn, where the lane turns. I can hear the stream from there, and the night is quiet. I do not know what it is called, but it is my home.

A hollow in the old ash by the stream. I have been there for many years, and I have raised my owlets there. The ash is hollowed out by the roots, and I can sit inside it with my wings folded. The stream runs past it, and I can hear the water all night. It is quiet there, and I can hear the wind in the leaves. I have no need to move far from my home. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

My home is the hollow in the old oak by the stream. It is deep and dry, and I have lined it with leaves and feathers. I have nested there for three years now, and the wood is warm under my wings. The stream runs beside it, and I can hear the water all night long. I do not know the name of this place, but I know it is mine. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.
My home is the hollow in the old oak. It is dry and warm in the summer, and I keep it clean. I have a few feathers in it, and I sleep on a dry leaf. I come and go through the ivy.

My home is the hollow in the old ash tree. It is deep and dry, and I have lined it with moss and leaves. I sleep there, and so do my mate and our young. We are safe there, and the wind does not carry us away.

I live in the hollow of an old ash tree, high in the wood. The tree is thick with ivy and the bark is cracked. I roost in the hollow, and the ivy keeps the wind out. A hollow in the old ash tree by the stream. The bark is thick and the leaves are gone. I have a nest of twigs and feathers. I keep it warm with my body. The wind comes through the cracks in the winter. I am used to it. It is the only place I can be still.
